title: Παιδίον ἐσθίον σπλάγχνα
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 292. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Βοτῆρες ἐπ’ ἀγρῷ θύοντες αἶγα τοὺς σύνεγγυς ἐκάλεσαν.
sentences.tr: Botēres ep’ agrōi thyontes aiga tous synengys ekalesan.
sentences.l: Herdsmen sacrificing a goat in the country called in those near by.
sentences.n: A sacrifice was a meal: the beast is killed, the god's portion burnt, and the rest eaten on the spot, so calling in the neighbours belongs to the rite rather than to hospitality. The same scene of a goat sacrificed in the country turns up again in fable 3. οἱ σύνεγγυς, 'those close at hand', is an adverb doing the work of a noun under its article.

sentences.t: Σὺν αὐτοῖς δὲ ἦν καὶ γυνὴ πενιχρά, μεθ’ ἧς καὶ ὁ παῖς αὐτῆς.
sentences.tr: Syn autois de ēn kai gynē penichra, meth’ hēs kai ho pais autēs.
sentences.l: And with them there was also a poor woman, and with her her child as well.
sentences.n: The relative clause has no verb of its own: ἦν is carried over from the main clause, as Greek regularly leaves the copula to be understood.

sentences.t: Προϊούσης δὲ τῆς εὐωχίας, τὸ παιδίον ὀγκωθὲν τὴν γαστέρα ἐκ τῶν κρεῶν, ὀδυνώμενον ἔλεγεν· « Ὦ μῆτερ, τὰ σπλάγχνα ἐμῶ. »
sentences.tr: Proiousēs de tēs euōchias, to paidion onkōthen tēn gastera ek tōn kreōn, odynōmenon elegen· « Ō mēter, ta splanchna emō. »
sentences.l: And the feasting going forward, the little child, swollen as to its belly from the meats, in pain was saying: « O mother, I am vomiting up my entrails. »
sentences.i: As the feast went on, the child, its belly swollen with the meat, said in its pain: « Mother, I am bringing up my entrails. »
sentences.n: τὴν γαστέρα is an accusative of respect with the passive participle ὀγκωθέν, 'swollen as to the belly' (the same turn as at fable 181). σπλάγχνα carries both senses at once: a person's own inward parts, and the victim's inner organs, which at a sacrifice are roasted first and shared out among the worshippers while the god gets the thigh-bones in fat. The whole point of the fable hangs on that one word doing two jobs.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ μήτηρ αὐτοῦ εἶπεν· « Οὐχὶ τὰ σά, τέκνον, ἃ δὲ κατέφαγες. »
sentences.tr: Hē de mētēr autou eipen· « Ouchi ta sa, teknon, ha de katephages. »
sentences.l: And his mother said: « Not your own, child, but those which you devoured. »
sentences.n: The relative ἅ has no antecedent expressed — 'but [those] which you ate up' — and κατεσθίω is the compound of eating a thing right down.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος οὗτος πρὸς ἄνδρα χρεωφειλέτην, ὅστις ἑτοίμως τὰ ἀλλότρια λαμβάνων, ὅταν ἀπαιτηθῇ ταῦτα, οὕτως ἄχθεται ὥσπερ ἐὰν οἴκοθεν ταῦτα ἐδίδου.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos houtos pros andra chreōpheiletēn, hostis hetoimōs ta allotria lambanōn, hotan apaitēthēi tauta, houtōs achthetai hōsper ean oikothen tauta edidou.
sentences.l: This fable is directed at a man in debt, who, readily taking what belongs to others, whenever he is asked these things back, is as vexed as if he were giving them out of his own house.
sentences.i: This fable is directed at the debtor who takes other people's goods readily enough and then, when they are called in, is as aggrieved as though he were paying out of his own store.
sentences.n: πρός with the accusative and no verb names the sort of man the fable is aimed at, the copula left unexpressed (as at fable 43). ἀπαιτηθῇ is passive and still keeps ταῦτα in the accusative: a verb with two objects can hold the second one when it goes passive (as at fable 10). ὅταν with the subjunctive makes it a rule rather than an occasion, 'whenever'. ὥσπερ ἐάν here stands for the ordinary ὥσπερ ἂν εἰ of unreal comparison, and the imperfect ἐδίδου gives it, 'as if he were giving'.
